en: The *Sarvāstivāda-pañcavastu-śāstra*,
translated by the Tripitaka Master and Śramaṇa Facheng, a Virtuous One from the Great Fan Country,
at the Dharma-hall of Xudu Monastery in Ganzhou.
There are five kinds of phenomena:
first, material phenomena;
second, mental phenomena.
Third, mental factors (caitta-dharma);
fourth, formations dissociated from mind (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra-dharma);
fifth, unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta-dharma).
What are material phenomena?
They refer to all those forms produced from the four great elements and derived from the four great elements.
What are the four great elements?
The earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element.
What is called derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*)?

It refers to the eye faculty, the ear faculty, the nose faculty, the tongue faculty, and the body faculty; all visible forms, sounds, odors, and tastes; and a portion of the tangible, together with non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*).
What are called mental phenomena?
They are mind, mentation, and consciousness.
Furthermore, what is meant by the sixfold body of consciousness: eye-consciousness, ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness?
What are called mental factors (caitta)?
They are those phenomena that are associated with the mind (citta). What, then, are they?

These are: feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention, desire, resolve, faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, applied thought, sustained thought, negligence, non-negligence, the roots of goodness, the roots of unwholesomeness, the roots of the indeterminate, the fetters, the bonds, the subtle and the gross, the secondary afflictions, the entanglements, abiding, knowledge, vision, all forms of clear realization, and whatever other dharmas are associated with the mind—such categories as these are called mental factors (caitta-dharma).
What are called the formations dissociated from mind?
They are those dharmas that are not associated with the mind.
Furthermore, what are they?

These are: acquisition (*prāpti*), the attainment of signlessness (*animittasamāpatti*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the state of signlessness (*animitta*), the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the homogeneous character of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*), the acquisition of a location, the acquisition of an object, the acquisition of a place, birth (*jāti*), aging (*jarā*), duration (*sthiti*), impermanence (*anityatā*), the group of names (*nāmakāya*), the group of phrases (*padakāya*), and the group of phonemes (*vyañjanakāya*). Furthermore, there are other dharmas that are dissociated from the mind; such categories as these are called the formations dissociated from the mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāradharma*).
What is called unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*)?
It refers to the three kinds of unconditioned:
space (*ākāśa*), cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); these are called unconditioned phenomena.
What is the earth element?
It is solidity and hardness.
What is the water element?
It refers to the nature of being thin and moist.
What is the fire element?
It refers to the nature of heat and warmth.
What is the wind element?
It is the nature of lightness and movement.
What is the eye faculty?
This refers to the pure matter that serves as the basis for visual consciousness.
What is the ear faculty?
It refers to the pure matter that serves as the basis for auditory consciousness.
What is the nose faculty?
It refers to the translucent matter that serves as the basis for nose-consciousness.
What is the tongue faculty?
That is to say, it is the pure matter upon which tongue-consciousness depends.
What is the body-faculty?
It is the pure matter upon which body-consciousness depends.
What are all forms?

They refer to beautiful forms, unattractive forms, and the forms that abide between those two, as well as manifest colors and so forth; these are initially known by the first consciousness—the eye-consciousness—and experienced by the eye-consciousness, while being cognized by the mental consciousness.
Therefore, all forms are cognized by two types of consciousness: eye-consciousness and mental-consciousness.
What are sounds? There are two kinds of sound:
those produced from the primary elements that are appropriated (*upātta-mahābhūta-hetuka*), and those produced from the primary elements that are not appropriated (*anupātta-mahābhūta-hetuka*).
The very first consciousness—the ear-consciousness—cognizes and receives the sound, which the mental consciousness (mano-vijñāna) is then able to cognize.
Therefore, all sounds are cognized by two consciousnesses: the ear-consciousness and the mental consciousness.
What are the various fragrances?
They are pleasant fragrances, unpleasant fragrances, and neutral fragrances.

The first of these is known by the nose-consciousness (*ghrāṇavijñāna*), experienced by the nose-consciousness, and cognized by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). Therefore, these various fragrances are apprehended by two consciousnesses: the nose-consciousness and the mental consciousness.
What are the various tastes?
They are those that are agreeable, disagreeable, and neutral.
Initially, they are known by the tongue-consciousness, experienced by the tongue-consciousness, and subsequently cognized by the mental consciousness.
Therefore, all tastes are cognized by two types of consciousness: tongue-consciousness and mental-consciousness.
What is the portion of the tangible?
It refers to smoothness, roughness, lightness, heaviness, cold, hunger, thirst, and so forth.
The first consciousness is that which is known by body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*), received by body-consciousness, and cognized by mental-consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Therefore, a portion of all contacts (*sparśa*) is cognized by these two consciousnesses: body-consciousness and mental-consciousness.
What are called the various unmanifest forms (*avijñaptirūpa*)?
They are the forms included within the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), which at all times are cognized solely by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
What is visual consciousness?
It is that which, depending upon the eye faculty, individually cognizes forms.
What is auditory consciousness?
Relying on the ear faculty, one individually cognizes sounds.
What is nose-consciousness?
Relying on the nose faculty, one individually cognizes odors.
What is tongue-consciousness?
It is that which, depending on the tongue-faculty, individually cognizes tastes.
What is body-consciousness?
Based on the body faculty (*kāyendriya*), one individually cognizes tangibles (*spraṣṭavya*).
What is the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*)?
Based on the mind faculty (*manendriya*), one individually cognizes phenomena (*dharma*).
What is feeling (*vedanā*)?
It is the nature of experiencing.
This is further divided into three types: suffering, pleasure, and that which is neither suffering nor pleasure.
What is perception?
It is the nature of thorough knowledge.
This, moreover, is of three kinds:
Small, great, and immeasurable.
What is volition?
It refers to the mental formations created by the mind and the actions performed by the intellect.
This, moreover, is of three kinds: namely, wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate.
What is contact? It is the conjunction of the three.
This, moreover, is threefold:
the experience of pleasure, the experience of suffering, and the experience of neither-suffering-nor-pleasure.
What is mental attention?
It refers to the transformation of the mind.
This, moreover, is of three kinds: that of the learner (*śaikṣa*), that of the one beyond learning (*aśaikṣa*), and that which is neither of the learner nor beyond learning.
What is desire?
It refers to the nature of delighting in action.
What is resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*)?
It refers to that which the mind delights in, the state of delighting, and the nature of delighting in action.
What is faith?
It is the utter purity of the mind.
What is diligence?
It refers to the mind’s inclination toward delight.
What is mindfulness? It is the nature of the mind to clearly retain [objects] in memory.
What is concentration?
It is one-pointedness of mind. What is wisdom?
This refers to the investigation of dharmas (*dharmapravicaya*). What is vitarka?
Its nature is mental coarseness (*audārikatā*).
What is investigation (*vicāra*)?
Its nature is mental subtlety.
What is heedlessness (*pramāda*)?
If one does not cultivate various virtues,
how can there be non-negligence? It is said that non-negligence consists in cultivating various virtues.
The roots of goodness refer to the three roots of goodness:
the root of non-attachment, the root of non-hatred, and the root of non-delusion.
The roots of unwholesomeness refer to the three roots of unwholesomeness: [greed, hatred, and delusion].
The unwholesome roots are greed, hatred, and delusion.
As for the indeterminate roots, there are four indeterminate roots, namely: indeterminate craving, views, conceit, and ignorance.
What is neutral craving?
It refers to the five types of activity pertaining to the realms of form and formlessness.
What is neutral view?
This refers to the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and the view of extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi) operative within the desire realm, as well as the five views operative within the form and formless realms.
What is neutral pride?
It refers to the five types of pride operative within the form and formless realms.
What is indeterminate ignorance?

It refers to the ignorance associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) as they function within the desire realm, as well as the five types [of ignorance] that function within the form and formless realms.
Regarding the "fetters" (*saṃyojana*), they refer to nine kinds of fetters:

the fetter of greed, the fetter of hostility, the fetter of pride, the fetter of ignorance, the fetter of views, the fetter of clinging to excellence, the fetter of doubt, the fetter of envy, and the fetter of avarice.
What is the fetter of greed?
It refers to greed for the three realms.
What is the fetter of ill will?
Based on the nature of anger and resentment in sentient beings, what is the fetter of pride (*māna-saṃyojana*)?

It refers to the seven types of pride, which are called the fetter of pride: namely, pride (*māna*), excessive pride (*atimāna*), pride beyond pride (*mānātimāna*), the pride of self (*asmimāna*), overweening pride (*adhimāna*), inferiority pride (*ūnamāna*), and false pride (*mithyāmāna*).
What is pride (*māna*)? It is to consider oneself superior when one is inferior, or to consider oneself equal when one is equal.
Taking that as a cause, it is the state of being sustained by pride, the loftiness of the mind, the arrogance of the mind, and the grasping of the mind; this is called pride.
What is overweening pride (*adhimāna*)?
It is to consider oneself superior to those who are equal, or to consider oneself equal to those who are superior;
taking this as a cause, it is the specific nature of pride, the loftiness of the mind, the haughtiness of the mind, and the fixation of the mind—this is called overweening pride.
What is the conceit of "I am"?

It refers to observing the five aggregates of clinging as either "I" or "mine. With that as its cause, it is the state of being conceited and haughty, the loftiness of mind, the arrogance of mind, and the grasping of mind; this is called the conceit of "I am."
What is overweening pride (*adhimāna*)?

It refers to one who, regarding a superior excellence not yet attained, reckons themselves as having attained that superior excellence; or, regarding a superior excellence not yet realized, touched, or manifested, reckons themselves as having realized it. Taking that as a cause, there arises a state of haughtiness and the nature of pride—a loftiness of mind, an arrogance of mind, and a fixation of mind. This is called overweening pride.
What is the pride of inferiority (*ūnamāna*)?

It refers to the estimation of oneself as slightly inferior when one is actually much more excellent; taking that as a cause, it is the state of being conceited and arrogant, the loftiness of mind, the haughtiness of mind, and the clinging of mind—this is called the pride of inferiority.
What is false pride (*mithyāmāna*)?

It refers to one who, while lacking virtuous qualities, conceives themselves as possessing them; taking that as a cause, it is a state of arrogance and haughtiness, an elevation of the mind, a disdain of the mind, and a fixation of the mind—this is called false pride.
These seven types of conceit are called the fetter of conceit (*māna-saṃyojana*).
What is the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*)?
It refers to the lack of knowledge regarding the three realms; this is called the fetter of ignorance.
What is the fetter of views?
It refers to three types of fetters called the fetter of views.
What are these three?
1. The view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi);
2. The view of extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi);
3. False view (mithyādṛṣṭi).
What is the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*)?

It refers to observing the five aggregates of clinging as either "I" or "mine. Taking that as its cause, the acceptance, inclination, wisdom, observation, and views [so formed] are called the view of a self-identity.
What is the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*)?

It refers to the contemplation of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*) as either annihilated or eternal; taking those as its cause, it consists of acceptance, inclination, wisdom, observation, and the resulting view—this is called the view of extremes.
What is wrong view?

It refers to the denial of cause and effect, as well as the negation of functional activity and existing phenomena; taking these as one's basis, whatever acceptance, delight, wisdom, contemplation, and perspective one holds is called wrong view.
These three types of views are called the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*).
What is the fetter of adherence to excellence (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*)?
The two kinds of adherence to excellence are called the fetter of adherence to excellence.
What are the two?
First, the adherence to views as supreme;
second, the adherence to precepts and observances as supreme.
What is the view of holding as supreme?

It refers to regarding the five aggregates of clinging as the most excellent, the highest, the superior, and the ultimate; taking that as a cause, one’s acceptance, delight, wisdom, contemplation, and vision—this is called the view of holding as supreme.
What is the grasping at rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*)?

It refers to regarding the five aggregates of clinging as pure, as liberation, or as transcendence; taking that as a cause, one’s acceptance, pleasure, wisdom, contemplation, and views—this is called the grasping at rules and observances.
These two kinds of superior grasping are called the fetter of superior attachment (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*).
What is the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*)?
It is characterized by hesitation regarding the [Four] Truths.
What is the fetter of restlessness?
Its nature is mental agitation.
What is the fetter of stinginess?
The mind takes them as its inherent nature;
therefore, they are called "fetters" (saṃyojana).
As for what is called "bondage," those very fetters that have been described are also termed "bonds" (bandhana).
However, there are three kinds of fetters, namely the fetter of greed, the fetter of hatred, and the fetter of delusion; therefore, they are called "fetters.
As for "subtle and extensive," this refers to the seven subtle and extensive [realms].
What are the seven?
First, the subtle and pervasive nature of greed;
second, the subtle and pervasive nature of anger; [and so forth].
3. The slight predominance of desire;
4. the slight predominance of pride;
5. the slight predominance of ignorance.
Sixth, the expansion of views;
seventh, the expansion of doubt.
What is the expansion of greed?
The five types of subtle and extensive [craving] are called "subtle and extensive craving. What are these five? They are:

all craving associated with the desire realm that is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering; and all craving associated with the desire realm that is to be abandoned through the vision of the origin, the cessation, and the path, as well as through cultivation.
These five kinds of pervasiveness are called the pervasiveness of greed.
What is the pervasiveness of hatred?
These five kinds of pervasiveness are called the pervasiveness of hatred.
What are the five? They are:

all forms of hatred abandoned through the vision of suffering; and all forms of hatred abandoned through the vision of the origin, the cessation, and the path, as well as those abandoned through cultivation.
These five minor pervasions are called the minor pervasion of aversion.
What is the minor pervasion of sensual desire?
These ten minor pervasions are called the minor pervasion of sensual desire.
What are the ten?
They are the five bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) and the five bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
What are called the five bound to the realm of form that are subtle yet extensive and accompanied by craving?

This refers to all craving associated with the form realm that is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, as well as all craving associated with the form realm that is to be abandoned through the vision of origin, cessation, and the path, and through cultivation.
Just as there are five [types] bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), so too are there five bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
These ten subtle expansions (*anu-vistara*) are called the "subtle expansions with desire" (*sāmiṣa-anu-vistara*).
What are the "subtle expansions of conceit" (*māna-anu-vistara*)?
These fifteen types of subtle and extensive [manifestations] are called the subtle and extensive manifestations of pride (*māna*). What are the fifteen?
They are the five bound to the desire realm, the five bound to the form realm, and the five bound to the formless realm.
What are called the five types of subtle pride associated with the desire realm?

They are all forms of pride associated with the desire realm that are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering; and all forms of pride associated with the desire realm that are to be abandoned through the vision of the origin, the cessation, and the path, as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation.
Just as there are five types bound to the desire realm, so too are there five bound to the form realm and five bound to the formless realm.
These fifteen kinds of subtle expansion are called the "subtle expansion of pride."
What is the subtle and extensive nature of ignorance?
These fifteen kinds of subtlety and extensiveness constitute the subtle and extensive nature of ignorance.
What are the fifteen?
This refers to the five types bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the five bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and the five bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
What are called the five kinds of subtle pride (*māna*) bound to the desire realm?

They are all the luminances (*āloka*) belonging to what is bound to the desire realm and abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), as well as all the luminances belonging to what is bound to the desire realm and abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudaya*), cessation (*nirodha*), and the path (*mārga*), and through cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
Just as there are five [types] bound to the desire realm, so too are there five bound to the form realm and five bound to the formless realm.
These fifteen kinds of subtle and extensive [states] are called the subtle and extensive ignorance (*avidyā-audārika*).
What is the vision of the subtle and vast?
It is said that the thirty-six subtle and vast [factors] constitute the vision of the subtle and vast.
What are these thirty-six?
That is to say: twelve [factors] bound to the desire realm, twelve bound to the form realm, and twelve bound to the formless realm.
What are the twelve views broadly explained as being bound to the desire realm?

That is to say: the view of a self-identity and the view of extremes bound to the desire realm; all false views and dogmatic attachment to views bound to the desire realm that are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering; all false views and dogmatic attachment to views bound to the desire realm that are to be abandoned through the vision of cessation; and all false views, dogmatic attachment to views, and adherence to rules and observances bound to the desire realm that are to be abandoned through the vision of the path.
Just as there are twelve [factors] bound to the desire realm, so too are there twelve bound to the form realm and twelve bound to the formless realm.
These thirty-six subtle expansions are called the "subtle expansion of views."
What is the "subtle and extensive" aspect of doubt?
The twelve kinds of subtle and extensive aspects are called the subtle and extensive aspect of doubt.
What are these twelve?
This refers to the four [types of doubt] bound to the desire realm, the four bound to the form realm, and the four bound to the formless realm.
What are called the four subtle and extensive doubts bound to the desire realm? They are:

the doubt to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha) that is bound to the desire realm, and the various doubts bound to the desire realm that are to be abandoned through the vision of origin (samudaya), cessation (nirodha), and the path (mārga).
Just as it is with those bound to the desire realm, so it is for those bound to the form realm and those bound to the formless realm, each having four;
these twelve types of subtle pervasiveness are called the "subtle pervasiveness of doubt."
Therefore, they are called "subtle and extensive.

Regarding the phrase "all secondary afflictions" (*upakleśa*): whatever is subtle and extensive is designated as "all secondary afflictions. However, there are things that are secondary afflictions which are not subtle and extensive;
namely, with the exception of those that are subtle and extensive, all other defiled formations within the aggregate of mental factors (*citta-saṃskāra-skandha*) produced by the mind.
"Abiding in entanglement" refers to abiding in eight kinds of entanglements.
What are the eight?
First, torpor;...
2. Sleep; 3. Restlessness; 4. Remorse;
5. Envy; 6. Avarice; 7. Lack of shame;
Eight?
Lack of shame.
Therefore, it is called "dwelling in entanglement."
Regarding "knowledge," it refers to ten kinds of knowledge.
What are the ten?
First, dharma-knowledge;
2. Knowledge conforming to [the knowledge of] others' minds;
3. Knowledge of others' minds;
4. Conventional knowledge;
5. Knowledge of suffering;
6. Knowledge of the origin;
7. Knowledge of cessation;
8. Knowledge of the path;
9. Knowledge of exhaustion;
10. Knowledge of non-arising.
What is the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna)?

It refers to the untainted knowledge regarding all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) bound to the desire realm; the untainted knowledge regarding the causes of conditioned phenomena bound to the desire realm; the untainted knowledge regarding the cessation of conditioned phenomena bound to the desire realm; and the untainted knowledge within the path that abandons conditioned phenomena bound to the desire realm.
Furthermore, regarding dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*): the various untainted knowledges within the stage of dharma-knowledge are called dharma-knowledge.
What is subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*)?

It refers to the various untainted knowledges regarding the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) bound to the realms of form and formlessness; the various untainted knowledges regarding the cessation of the conditioned phenomena bound to the realms of form and formlessness; and the various untainted knowledges regarding the path of abandonment for the conditioned phenomena bound to the realms of form and formlessness.

Furthermore, the various untainted knowledges (*anāsrava-jñāna*) that correspond to the specific objects understood and the stages (*bhūmi*) in which they are understood—these are called "subsequent knowledges" (*anvaya-jñāna*).
What is the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*)?

From the wisdom born of cultivation, the fruit of that which has been cultivated is attained without regression based upon what was practiced; by means of this wisdom, one understands the mental activities of others in the realms of desire and form, including their minds and mental factors, and realizes a portion of the untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas before one’s eyes—these are termed the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
What is conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*)?
It refers to contaminated knowledge (*sāsravajñāna*); this is called conventional knowledge.
What is the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*)?
The untainted wisdom produced through mental attention that realizes the five aggregates of clinging as being impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self is called the knowledge of suffering.
What is the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*)?

It is the untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) that attends to the causes of tainted phenomena (*sāsrava-hetu*) as being their origination, accumulation, arising, and condition; this is called the knowledge of origination.
What is the knowledge of cessation?
It refers to the untainted wisdom that arises regarding cessation by attending to it as cessation, tranquility, excellence, and renunciation; this is called the knowledge of cessation.
What is the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*)?

It refers to the untainted wisdom (*anāsravajñāna*) that arises regarding the path, consisting of the mental orientations (*manasikāra*) of "this is the path," "this is the reality," "this is the practice," and "this is the departure. This is called the knowledge of the path.

What is the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*)? It refers to the thorough and complete knowledge of suffering for oneself; the self-knowledge of having abandoned the origin of suffering; the self-knowledge of having realized cessation; and the self-knowledge of having cultivated the path. Taking these as its cause, it is the clear and distinct comprehension through knowledge, vision, awakening, and wisdom, which is directly realized before one; this is called the knowledge of exhaustion.
What is the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*)?
It refers to the knowledge that there is nothing further to be known, because one has personally and thoroughly understood all suffering;
and the knowledge that there is nothing further to be abandoned, because one has personally severed the origin of suffering.
Because self-realization has ceased, there is no further wisdom to be realized;
because the path has been cultivated by oneself, there is no further wisdom to be cultivated.

Taking this as its cause, one’s knowledge, vision, awakening, and discernment become clear and distinct, attaining realization in the present moment; this is called the "knowledge of non-arising" (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
Regarding the term "view" (*dṛṣṭi*): although that wisdom is indeed a view, there are also views that are not wisdom.

The eight types of receptivity (*kṣānti*) arising from the limit of clear observation (*abhisamaya*)—namely, the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*), the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*), the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of origination (*samudaya-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*), the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of origination (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*), the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of cessation (*nirodha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*), the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*), the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of the path (*mārga-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*), and the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*)—are therefore called "views."
Regarding what is called "clear realization" (abhisamaya): that very knowledge and vision is itself clear realization; therefore, it is termed "clear realization.
What is meant by "attainment"?
It refers to that which is acquired among all phenomena.
What is the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*)?

It is defined as the cessation of mind and mental factors, preceded by the mental attention of the perception of renunciation, occurring when one has already abandoned craving for the Realm of Universal Purity (*śubhakṛtsna*) but has not yet abandoned craving for the higher realms.
What is the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*)?

It is defined as the nature of the cessation of mind and mental factors, occurring in one who has already become detached from the craving for the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), preceded by the mental attention to the perception of cessation.
What is the possession of non-conception?
It refers to that which has the nature of the cessation of mind and mental factors upon being born among the sentient beings of the Heaven of Non-conception.
What is the life-faculty?
This refers to the life-span within the three realms.
What is the "homogeneity of beings" (nikāya-sabhāga)?
It refers to the mutual similarity among sentient beings of their own kind.
What is meant by "attaining a location"?
It refers to obtaining various objects.
What is meant by "attaining a thing"?
This refers to the acquisition of the aggregates (*skandha*).
What is the acquisition of the bases (*āyatana*)?
It refers to the acquisition of the internal and external bases.
What is birth? It is the manifestation of the aggregates. What is aging?
It refers to the maturation of the aggregates.
What is stability? It refers to the non-destruction of conditioned phenomena.
What is impermanence? It is the disintegration of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
What is called the "name-body" (*nāmakāya*)?
That is precisely the "designation" (adhivacana).
What is a "phrase-group" (padakāya)?
It refers to the completion of syllables (vyañjana).
What is the body of phonemes (*vyañjana-kāya*)?
It is precisely that body of syllables (*akṣara-kāya*) which is called the body of phonemes.
What is space (*ākāśa*)?
The cause of that which is traversed is space itself; it is without obstruction, and no variety of material forms can completely cover it—this is called space.
What is non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)?
This refers to cessation that is not dissociation.
What is analytical cessation?
It refers to cessation that is also dissociation.
Therefore, it is said that there are five kinds of phenomena (*dharma*):
first, material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*);
second, mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*).
Third, mental factors (caitta-dharma);
fourth, formations dissociated from mind (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra-dharma);
fifth, unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta-dharma).
*Pañcavastuka-śāstra*, one fascicle.
